speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Hi, thank you so much for joining me today. I'd love to start with having you state your name and your pronouns, and where you're currently located.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: Yeah, my name is Dr. KáLyn Coghill, my pronouns are she, they, and I'm located in Richmond, Virginia.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Awesome. And then, are you from Richmond originally, or did you move there at a different time?

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: No, I was born in Richmond, Virginia, but I also spent, half of my life on the West Coast, mainly in Northern California and the Bay Area.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Okay, did your, your family, like, your folks, did they grow up in Richmond as well?

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: Yes, both sides of my family, starting with my, grandparents, and their parents came here, but most of everyone is from, Richmond, Virginia, or they are from King and Queen County. Which is also in Virginia. It's, like, 30 minutes away from Richmond.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Okay, okay, cool. And what was, your family like, like, growing up? Can you talk a little bit about what family looks like and means to you?

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: Yeah, so, I, have come to defining family more so in my mid to late 30s, rather than having a full understanding growing up. I was a ward of the state. My father was murdered when I was six, and my mom was also very much so involved in street life, so, I kind of, like, moved around with different family members, was kind of just shipped around, so, for me, most of my, I guess, like, view of what a family is supposed to be was mainly what I maybe saw on television, or, like, if I was reading a book, or if, like, friends invited me over to their home.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: But as far as, in my own family, I never really had a clear view or understanding of what it means to be a part of a family. So for me, understanding what, like, family and, like, a familial bond is became clearer for me as I was becoming an adult, and also creating my own type of family amongst, like, my friends and other folks that I'm in community with.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: So, that kind of leads me down two different paths. Like, on one hand, I'm really interested in hearing about how you have kind of formed chosen family, and I'm also interested in how you… what your relationship to, like, ancestry and lineage looks like as you've gotten older and started to think about family in different ways. Yeah.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: Yeah, so, I can answer the second question first. So, I started doing ancestral veneration without knowing what it was when my father passed, so I was about 7. And that's just something that, like, my mother, when she had custody of me at the time, like, she, like, gave me a picture of him when, like, his, high school photo, and for me, it was more so that she was like, "Oh, you know, you should talk to this photo. You know, you should engage with this photo of your father, even though he's not here." So for me, that's when I really started actually, like, thinking about, what it means to talk back to those who have passed on, so that started at a very, very young age. And I continue doing those practices, throughout most of my life.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: By the time I went off to college, I had learned a lot about my ancestry and lineage from one of my great-aunts. Her name is, Everdeen. She's no longer with us, but she was the family member who was, who I most admired, and the way that she, like, unapologetically talked about, that side of my family, which is my maternal… paternal side of that family, their lineage, from whether it was good, bad, ugly, and a lot of family members would equate that to her, you know... having mental health issues, or, you know, like, "oh, you know, she's, you know, moved up north now, so she's, like, trying to act different," but for me, that was grounding for me to fully understand, like, where I came from on that side of my family.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: And because, that side of my family is Indigenous and Black, I learned a lot about just Indigenous culture and Blackness in rural life at a very, very young age. Through my Aunt Everdeen, from going to, like, like, family cookouts and stuff, and, like, being in that environment, and kind of just sitting around and listening to adults talk. And it continued to foster a desire for me to really understand what it means to not only venerate your ancestors, but really use them as a guiding force.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: And, as I, you know, graduated from undergrad and, like, you know, got older, I became more, I guess, advanced in veneration, right? Because I had more tooling, I had money. So, I was really leaning into, like, a lot of practices around hoodoo and, like, herbalism because of me being Indigenous and also Black. And I know that there were a lot of medicine women on that side of my family, so, like, really, like, honing in on my gifts, and the ways that I was able to hone in on those gifts was by really tapping into my ancestors, so… Paying very, like, close attention to, like talking to them, and doing, like, a lot of asking questions if I could get answers from folks, making sure that I was being very intentional with choices that I was making in reference to what I knew about my ancestors, but also what I didn't want to repeat from what I had learned. And then now, that I am, you know, getting closer to 40, I started really leaning into my, my religious practicing, which requires ancestral veneration, I practice in ATR [African Traditional Religion], I'm an Ìṣẹ̀ṣe practitioner, and as a child of Ọ̀ṣun and Ọ̀bàtálá, like, I… out, like, it's almost like a requirement when you're practicing, like, an African tradition religion, right, to know how to venerate your ancestors first, right? Like, the Orishas and everything, of course, are important, but if you do not do the veneration, if you do not have an ancestor altar, if you are not tending to that, then all of the other things that will show up, particularly in Ìṣẹ̀ṣe for you, the understandings, the learnings, even those particular blessings, will be blocked because they want you to be able to venerate your ancestors.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: Right? So, for me, I would say ancestral veneration, starting with the passing of my father, was even though I was really, really young, that was extremely important. Like, I still have the photo that my mom gave me, like, I've… and mind you, I said I was awarded the state eventually, so I have no other documentations of my things. No childhood photos, things like that, but I still have that photo, it went everywhere that I went, and now I have, like, a beautiful altar in my apartment that has more photos, more, like, you can… I can tell how deep I am in, like, connecting with my ancestors based on, like, how my altar has grown, like, what my offerings look like, what I, like, really focus on as it pertains to, what I deem as important, and then also, like, how I choose what type of work I want to do, whether it is for my personal self, or even, like, career-wise.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Wow, that was such a beautiful answer, and so thorough. I really appreciate it, especially when you were talking about your religious practice and how that informs the relationship that you have to ancestry. And you started to answer this question, but I kind of wanted to circle back to it, to emphasize a little. Like, you talked a bit about being Indigenous. I was wondering how you identify, and, like, this can be both about race and ethnicity, but also about other parts of your identity that speak very strongly to you.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: Yeah, so, it's very funny that you're asking me this, because I was just talking, with a new co-worker who's also Indigenous and Black, and they are living here now, but they're not from where I'm from, and just kind of talking about how I had went to a bookstore over the weekend. It was my birthday last weekend, and I bought this book. It's a children's book by an author that I know here in Richmond that focuses on, like, explaining, like, magical hoodoo to, like, children, and I was just telling her, like, I collect a lot of children's books and read a lot of children's books that focus on, like, Black practices, and I think that, like, it's really hard to find a lot of books about people who are Black and Indigenous, for a lot of reasons, as we know why. But I will say, like, as far as my identities, like, I, obviously, am Black. There's no way around that. Like, there's never gonna be a day where someone's like, are you Black? I am Black, but I am also Indigenous. But because there is such a fraught relationship, specifically here in Virginia, with a lot of the tribes dealing with racism, it is very, very difficult to exist as a Black, Indigenous person, and because of that.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: I typically don't talk about being Indigenous unless I am around other folks who may be Indigenous, unless I am around people from the diaspora, and we're kind of just talking about it, or unless people are asking me about my lineage, because I want to be honest.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: As far as my other identities, I am non-binary, but I identify as a Black femme, as a Black woman, and… I also am a person living with disabilities as well, and I'm neurodivergent, and I would… I guess, like, I don't know if this would be considered, like, an identity to, like, non-Black folks, but for Black folks, like, I'm also… I have a gift. Or a gift, right? I, you know, I'm clairaudient, like, I have a spiritual gift, so I'm… I'm a spiritualist, a spiritual person, in general. So those are, like, the identities that, like, I carry with me. Every day.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Yeah, I definitely hear you. Now, something I'm really curious about, like, that you… that you brought up is how… you won't… You're more likely to talk about the Indigenous part of your identity when you're talking to other Black people from other parts of the diaspora or from the continent, and I'm wondering, like, what that has looked like for you when you're engaging with, specifically, Black people from the continent when you're talking about indigeneity.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: Yeah, so I think that it is… for me, I think it's… I really enjoy talking to folks from the continent, but just really anybody from the diaspora. So we have team members who are Surinamese, Guyanese, or, even, like, I have friends and stuff who are from all different parts of the diaspora, Haitian. I have a lot of really close friends who are from the continent, and I enjoy talking to them about that because they actually are interested in that, right? They actually want to have those conversations.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: I remember one time, my coworker, JD, who is Surinamese, and they're from the Netherlands, we were talking about, like, a talk they recently did, and, like, a talk that Rudy did, and I was like, you know, "I really love how you all talk about, like, your, Surinamese lineage when you're talking about the stories." Now, I was like… and I was like, "I feel like I wish I could do that, too." I was like, "but I'm just Black American." And JD was like. "I feel like we can kind of talk about that experience, because you could also be talking about your ancestors." So, really, like, pulling out of me that, like, your… "your Black American-ness, your Southernness, you also be having Indigenous heritage is also just as important as when I'm telling my story about my Surinamese great-grandma coming to the Netherlands, right? That story is important."

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: And I think that, like, talking to other folks from the diaspora is very affirming. And also it is… it, like allows me, at least, to talk about the… the pain points of being Indigenous and, like, not being identifiable or recognizable by other people because of the way that I look, and also not being able to get access to the same benefits as Indigenous people who don't look like me.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: So there's a big disconnect from my own culture, but it's really, really, like, refreshing to be able to, like, to talk to other folks who may have some experiences, or, are, like, comfortable having those, like, very hard conversations about, like, even what's happening in their particular cultures, right? About, like, the types of... the types of ways that people are siloed or isolated, or the types of ways that, like, the government or white supremacy, right, has really, like, or colonization has fed into, right, how people can even identify, or how people can show up, or who is considered what in their own communities. And I think, for me, that's really helpful, because in America, what I've noticed as a Black American, especially a Black American from Virginia, is that people associate being Indigenous with a certain… with certain, like features, like, "oh, your hair is dark and wavy and curly, right?" Like, or like, "oh, you're, you know, like, oh, your skin is, like, an interesting olive color." Like, it's very much so about desirability politics, right? And it's also… so that's within our own community.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: Outside of our community, depending on the tribe that you're a part of and where it's located, right, like, being multiracial, being, you know, a part of the Black community, looking like a Black person is definitely a barrier for you to be included in those Indigenous communities. It's also very clear that it's also a way that those who are, like, put on pedestals in media, in television, in academia, right, who are Indigenous, right? They look a certain way. Right?

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: So I think that talking to folks throughout the diaspora, for me, it's just really affirming, especially because, like I said, I don't lead with saying I'm Indigenous, especially, like, more so now, as an adult, because I've learned, unfortunately, that the way that I looked previously was what would determine, like, intercommunal, that, "oh yeah, you must be Indigenous because of what your hair looks like. Oh, your hair is long and wavy," or whatever like that, but not more so that, like, I'm Indigenous because of my kinship, I'm Indigenous because that particular land that my family has, like, owns also should be recognized as a part of the actual tribe that's having the powwow up the road, right? Like, that is what I'm saying when I'm Indigenous. I could give a fuck less about what you look like, because… who cares about that, right? So I think that, like, for me now, I'm just kind of more so careful, but I will say this when I'm in non-Black spaces.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: And, and I did a conference recently, and the team, the whole team was, like, watching. It was, like, it was virtual, but it was global, and I was talking about our moderation and stuff like that. Someone had asked, like, "oh, okay, like, you know, I do moderation for, like, Indigenous communities, blah, blah, blah, blah, like, do you all plan on moderating for, like, other communities in the future?" And I literally responded with, like, "I'm Indigenous and Black. We are moderating for Indigenous people." Because I wanted them to sit with what they were saying, right? They're not saying, like, oh, are you also going to be moderating for the harms that impact all Indigenous people, they're not looking at Black people as an… as a part of being Indigenous. So they don't think that those particular labels, anti-Black harassment, anti-Black rhetoric, white supremacy, misogynoir, can apply to an… to an Indigenous person, because Indigenous doesn't, in their view, doesn't mean Black.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Totally, totally. I mean, we're talking about triple, quadruple consciousness, not just double consciousness here. And I think a part of what made me really curious about this line, too, is… how they're, like... Having spent some time in Kenya and Southern Africa, like, how much overlap there is between a Black experience in Africa and Indigenous experiences here in America, and there's just so much overlap so many times, and so I was really curious to hear about what your experience had been there.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: Yeah, and you know, I think that, like, I was talking to somebody else yesterday, maybe, about this? I can't remember, but we were just talking about how it… how, like, it's so… like, the… Oh, my co-worker who's Indigenous, I said, the internet is so interesting to me, as I watch it evolve, because it's now giving Black people an opportunity to talk to people all over the world, and for us to have a very clear understanding of what others are experiencing in different places, and being able to make those connections across lands, across continents that we may have made connections of within our communities or in reading a book, but being able to have community with folks who live in places that you may never step foot in. Right? And then you go to these places, and they are willing to chat and talk about their experiences, and there's commonalities. Though… that, to me, is what's really beautiful, about what I'm, like, witnessing currently, with, like, this current iteration of what we're seeing with, like, internet and community building.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Yeah, that's beautiful. And I think, okay, so here's another, another piece. You were talking a bit about how, within the Black community, oftentimes, when people are talking about indigeneity, it's about how a person looks, rather than necessarily, like, a connection to a lineage, or a particular way of thinking about things. And so that makes me wonder: to you, what does it mean to be Black?

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: Oh, I love that question. So… I would say that… being Black… I feel like I wrote this down recently, but, like, to me, Being Black is both… I think I posted about it... Being Black, specifically a Black woman, It is being both… rep…

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: Let me pause. I want to grab my journal, because I want to read exactly what I wrote, so give me one second.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Yeah, no worries at all.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: Okay, I'm an avid, like, writer, so I was like, oh, I really want to read what I wrote, because I don't want to, like, misquote myself.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Yeah, that's...

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: Whoa. What was that right?

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: Okay, and this was in reference to after I had read the most recent Nicole Hannah Jones article that she did, where she was, like, basically, like, just doing an update of the decision that her and her husband made for her daughter to go to a segregated school in New York, and how that's, like, really impacted her child. And me just kind of processing what I was reading.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: So I basically just said that, like, to be Black is to both hold rage and a deep sadness, and a faith for what seems impossible. So that's… when I think about being Black, I think about… the… The ways in which rage, faith... And when I say faith, I don't mean religious faith, but just, like, faith, like the faith of a mustard seed, which we hear all the time, but I think about the ways in which rage, sadness, faith. And also… This… very, like… a deep… Belief, and something that has never been seen, or something that may feel impossible, but still being Black anyway. I don't know if that necessarily makes sense in reference to your question, but when I think about Blackness, that's what I think about. I think about the realities of the fact that, like, as a Black person, every day of my life, I feel rage and deep sadness, but I also feel faith in things that are impossible.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: Literally, like, Right? And I think that those… all of those things, for me at least, have to exist for me to… feel Black?

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: Right? Like, I don't want to… just only say, we should only focus on Black joy, or, like, we should only focus on Black death, right? I want to hold all of it at the same time. And for me, that is what it means to be Black.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Yeah, that's a beautiful, beautiful answer. I'm so glad that you grabbed the notebook to pull it out.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Yeah, I mean, okay, so moving from… From there, like, if you were to describe a kind of Black worldview, right? Particularly with the experiences that you've had with people from all over the diaspora, like: what would you consider to be, like, a fundamental, like idea to, like, a Black worldview or ontology.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: Hmm. Just so I'm clear, when you're saying worldview, are you saying more so of what my worldview is, or what I perceive as something that is... That connects all Black people, even if they are not necessarily aware of it.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Yeah, more the latter, yeah. And if you want to talk to the first one, too, but, like, the second one is… yeah.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: Yeah, so what I will say is that what I think, as far as, like, what is a, like, basic common denominator, to be for lack of better words, amongst all Black people, is that we all exist, right, in this space as being hyper-visible and invisible at the same time.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: And the reason why I asked for clarification on worldview is because I wanted to be clear that this worldview is also ignored. Even within the person, this worldview is also maybe be a subconscious thing that people may not recognize until they experience something extremely traumatic or witness something that like, jolts them, right? But no matter what anyone can… anyone says, I don't care what, like, your political affiliations are, I don't care how much you lean into respectability politics. Even those particular actions are because there is a common denominator that we know that we exist as hypervisible and invisible, and that really determines whether we realize it or not how we move through the world at different capacities, right? Depending on where we come from, but that is, like, a baseline from where I've… from where I sit, and what I think, and what I've noticed. And that's across the globe. Right? I don't think that's just a Black American experience. I think that's a Black experience.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Totally. Totally. I feel that so much, being here in Boulder. I don't know how much you walked around while you were out here, but that speaks to what it's like to be here in a way that feels particularly weird being in America, where it's like, you should be able to feel a little bit more at home, but then, you know, I come out here from... From Brooklyn, and it's, like, a huge, huge difference. And I think, too, about, like, "the nod," and how, like, that plays into this worldview, where it's, like "I am going to acknowledge your humanity, because I know that you're not getting that necessarily from all these other people around us. I'm gonna make sure that you know that I see you," you know? Yeah. Yeah.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Do you have, this has been a pretty tricky question as I've asked it in these interviews so far, but… Do you have a particular story that you want to tell that you feel like exemplifies your Black experience? I know that it's hard to, like, reduce an entire lifetime to just one end. Yeah.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: Yeah, let's see. Okay, so… because I'm thinking… I'm being, like, very intentional about, like, what experience I decide to share, because, I mean, it could go one of two ways. It could be something extremely, like, traumatic for someone, or it could be something that, you know, is, like, a joyous experience. But I think for me... Okay.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: My Black experience, summed up into one moment is something that I experienced Intra-communally, and outside of my community at the same time.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Sorry, can you… Repeat that last bit, just the internet.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: So, yeah, so, the Black experience that I'll be sharing for myself is something that I experienced… I've experienced it a lot, but experienced it intra-communally, right, within the Black community, but also outside of the Black community at the same time. Like, in tandem.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: And that particular experience is that when I was finishing my master's program, and I was at an HBCU when I was finishing my master's program, I decided to do the thesis route because I knew eventually I was going to want to go get my PhD. And I did everything, I wrote it, I sent it to everyone, they were supposed to review it. My committee consisted of two Black women, and then my advisor was a Southeast Asian man, and…

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: I had very different relationships with everyone on the committee, so the… my advisor, him and I were really in lockstep on the same page, because I was also a GA, so I was constantly in there, really helped me with my work. One of the committee members was the first person I met when I got to Bowie State, and I was originally in the English program, and she was the one that was like, "oh, I think this particular program would be better suited for the work that you're trying to do." Encouraged a lot of me, you know, went back to the continent a lot, like, brought me different things, very, very, like, pouring in. And the other person was a professor, wasn't someone who was very well-liked, Black woman, but she, seemingly, in that instance, was one of the few people who maybe had a clear view of what I was trying to do with my research.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: Got to the defense, and this is definitely not to scare you, because I know you're working on your master's, but got to the defense presentation. Mind you, everyone looks… is supposed to look at your thesis and everything before you show up, right? So, like, you… you're never supposed to go to the defense if you're not gonna pass it. That is just not how that process works. I go to the defense. A lot of the professors and friends that I have who were also at Bowie and the program had taught me, worked with the folks that I was in my committee, had graduated from the program or worked there, were there, did the presentation, everything went over well, we walk out.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: And then… Of course, they bring me back in, and they say that I failed. And the reason that they said that I failed, right... And it was very interesting, the two Black women didn't say anything until I directly asked them, but they had my advisor tell me I failed. And I could just tell by his demeanor that he was very uncomfortable saying that.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: So, I was like, what? Like, why did I fail? One of them said, the person who suggested for me to move to this program, was with me through the whole process, was like, we just don't think that, like, you're ready to graduate.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: And I was like, okay. And then the other person is like, "I just feel like, you know, you didn't, like you know, really dive into the chapter that I wrote on social media, and, like, I feel like there's a lot of, people that are missing in the work." And I kind of was just, like, defeated, so I left, but the graduate dean for the school at the time, and some of the other professors were in that hallway, because we were in the graduate building, and the dean was like, "whoa, what's going on?" Because I'm, like, hysterically crying, and they were like, "well, maybe you can try next, you know, to defend again," and I'm like, "girl, I have a job starting. Like, I'm not doing that." So, the graduate dean was like, "wait, you didn't pass? Like, why didn't you pass? Like, we… everyone checked off the thesis for you to get to this point." It became this big to-do where they had to bring in the department chair. And then, they had to remove everyone from my committee, and they had to just bring in random professors for me to redo my defense, the same day later. Right?

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: That entire process for me was the moment when I realized that it did not really matter what space I was in, whether that space was Black, whether that space was white... Academia, in particular quickly reminded me that at the end of the day, I am going to be seen as what people perceive me as when they are looking at me, by the way that I talk, from where I come from, from my background, for my experience, right? And they're gonna use that to make judgment calls on what they think I deserve and what I'm worthy of. And for me, that really illuminated how I had experienced my entire life from a child up until that point, and a lot of instances start coming up of where I had been in a very similar situation, even though it wasn't academia, whether it was in my family, whether it was in extracurriculars, whether it was in a church setting, whether it was, you know, in an elementary school, right? There was always a contention between Black and white folks, whether they were on the same side or not, of "does this Black girl deserve what she is working towards?" And we get to decide whether or not we think that we should give her this thing, not because she's qualified, but more so how it would make us look for us to provide charity for this Black girl.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: And that's really kind of what shaped up my Black experience, and unfortunately, I can't be confident in saying that, like, I still don't feel inklings of that in different environments. But… ever since that moment, I am very, very keen and learned very quickly that, like... One: It's not just your family. Two: it's not just white people and non-Black people. It's also… it can also be people within your own community, right? That's when I learned about "all skin folk and ain't your kinfolk. I was shocked, couldn't believe it, right?

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: And I think that, you know, what really was, like, the lasting impression was the lack of accountability, and then the amount of complete silence and disappearance from the two Black women in particular, who I literally have never heard of… heard from since then. It's been almost 10 years. And as a Black woman, in my Black experience, I can't disparage them, right? I cannot… fully… You know, crash out, drag, or whatever like that, because that experience solidified, and has continued to solidify that for my Black experience, I am only seen as, in certain environments, as good as they want me to be seen as. And if I'm mistreated because of maybe their status, or who they are, or because of the fact that, like, I don't want to shape other people's perspective of someone, I have to carry that with me and my Black experience everywhere I go. And, you know, and they, you know, for them. I don't know how they feel about it, because we never got a chance to talk about it.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: So I think that, like, that really shaped my Black experience, and I hate that I shared that particular experience, because I was like, oh, maybe I should've… shared something, very… more joyful, but I think that, like, that, for me, was a turning point. For sure.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Yeah, that's huge. I really appreciate you... You sharing that. Do you… I mean, if you want, you can also share another experience that feels joyful. You don't have to, but if you...

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: Yeah, no!

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: If you felt like you wanted to balance it or something.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: Yeah, what I'll say is that, like, to… It's not even, like, a counter experience, it's just the, like the rage and faith and deep sadness that I talk about being Black, right? The faith part, right, is that I have been able to be affirmed, right, in the work that I've done to focus on protecting other Black women and girls through my work, through my advocacy, through volunteering, because of that particular experience, how deeply it shaped me to, like, become more aggressive with how I do that and making that my priority. And I would say that one of the… the things that came from that rage and deep sadness and still the face to figure out something impossible is being able to work with, young people at Justice for Black Girls. I'm the assistant director for the Black Girlhood Fellowship Program. I'm also, like, on the board and the board chair, but being able to be in this space with them over the past 8 months to help them feel confident as researchers, to help them feel confident for asking the questions that people don't think is actually important research, right? To be able to actually, like, prepare to watch them next week present their research, right, in front of our academic network and our board, and to have, you know, 12 of them come to our conference in November and present their work in front of everyone including Beyoncé mama.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: So for me, right, like... I… That, for me, is the part of my Black experience that's that faith, like, I'm not presenting my shit in front of Miss Tina Knowles, I don't really need to do that, but the students that I get to work with, they get to share something that they thought they couldn't actually research because of not having possibility models, not having someone who actually was helping them, like become stronger researchers and stronger writers, was actually interested in cultivating, right, their skill set and encouraging them, that, for me, is, like, the part of my Black experience that is… that overshadows that particular experience. Because that particular experience could have basically been the end for a lot of people. They're like, you know what, I'm good. I don't want to do none of this other stuff. But for me, it was more so just, like, a very much clearer view on how I definitely need to move moving forward.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Totally, totally. Could you, could you, tell me a little bit about your research? Like, what you were studying at that time, and what you went to go do your PhD on?

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: Yeah, so, I… For the past 12 years, it started off with me… well, what is this, 2026? Or 13 years. It started off with me looking at, twitter, and… what… how, like, Black women were being treated, but what was the, like, catalyst for that was my own experience with, like, online harassment. At that time, I was just calling it digital violence towards Black women, because I was not aware of the term misogynoir, and it came out, like, there was one paper written in 2008. I was in my program in, like, 2014, so it was still very fresh. There wasn't a lot of research on Black Twitter at the time. Like, Meredith Clark and all of them literally were just, like, getting started. Right? So it was very much so, like, I was looking more so at, like, the criminology aspect, so looking at, like, Carolyn West's work, where she's talking about, like, how, like, violence and trauma, like, deeply impacts Black women, and me connecting that to the online experience.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: So what I've been doing for the better half of, well, basically most of my 20s and my 30s is, looking at digital misogynoir, and focusing on how that very, very specific anti-Black racism and sexism impacts women, femmes, and gender-expansive people in digital spaces, originally focusing solely on Twitter. And now, really, like, expanding, not necessarily my focus, right? Because when you're in your doc program or your master's program, you are trying to… you're looking at one specific thing, but that doesn't mean that, like, that specific issue or the… the thing that you're looking at is contained to that. That is just, like, what my particular focus was at that time. But really, like, trying to really continue to make these connections for people that, like digital misogynoir… misogynoir is a public health crisis. It physiologically impacts Black women, non-binary, and gender expansive people. It deeply impacts the physiological experiences of those observing it, those intervening it, even if they don't want to recognize it. It is the direct cause of the uptick of Black femicide, Black trans women being killed, how Black women are harmed online and offline, and… Making that connection to folks where, like, I've always talked about how it shows up online, right? But I've also always pressed people to understand that, like it's not just something that appeared on the internet. It's exasperated on the internet because of the lack of regulations, and also just the, the way that, like, anonymity can work, but these particular thought processes, these particular systems have been around for centuries, right? Like, I always in all of the work that I do, I always remind people that 400 years ago, when we were dragged over here, Black women were not considered human, right? Like, I need people to sit with that. We were not a part of the slave count. We were not human. We were deemed as unrapeable. You… there was no… the word rape was not attributed to what Black women experienced, right? That has deeply shaped how we are seeing things throughout history, but especially online. What we're seeing now is not new, so for me, my research focuses on, now, really, harm reduction as always, but also kind of just, like aggressively reminding people that, like, just because you are away from keyboard doesn't mean that you're away from violence. So…

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Wow, that, that's quotable right there. "Just because you're away from the keyboard doesn't mean you're away from violence." Yeah. Can you, can you talk about that harm reduction aspect? Like, what, yeah, can you just speak a little bit more to that?

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: Yeah, so… I'll do a... So, for my master's thesis in particular, I did a focus group, I was in the DC area, with Black women, and I used Leslie Jones' experience with the Ghostbuster rollout as basically, like, the case study. And what's so funny is, I was just telling another doc student that I met at Oakland Tech Week that, like, when I did my master's, the only theory I could find that I could attach to what Black women were experiencing online was muted group theory. It is a communications theory that is not well researched. There was not a lot of research on it, but that was the only one that kind of talked about what it means to, like, silence someone, right? So what I did was, in the focus group, I had them asking, like, answering a series of questions, but also looking at… at that time, Twitter had just released their Trust and Safety, like... I forgot what they were called at the time, but this was right after, like, Gamergate. They released, like, in 2016, these trust and safety guidelines, right? And… and their Trust and Safety Council, and they were, like, rolling out all this trust and safety stuff, and I had them look at that, and we talked about, like: is it vague? Does it make sense? We talked about, like, what they're experiencing online, how they're protecting their self online, and this was in 2016.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: And that master's thesis became my first publication, and then when I decided to go to get my PhD, between that time, because I always worked in between each degree and with every degree, but in between that time I was starting to do a lot of, like, speaking and stuff around, like, the experiences of Black women online, and really, like, talking to a lot of folks at these different, like, speaking… speaking environments and talking to other scholars about, like, the fact that, like... I'm… I, personally, am like "well, the only way this can be done is if they, like, if we work for Twitter, right?" That was my theory in 2016-2017. Got to my doc program in 2020, had a conversation with André Brock, we were, like, on the phone or something, and, like, I'm, like, going the fuck off, per usual, and André is like, well, you know, "I know, like, your whole dream has been to, like, literally take Twitter down, but I really think this is unhealthy for you." He was like, "I think that what you're really always focusing on is, like, how these Black women and femmes are creating harm reduction. Not necessarily, right: why the Black women aren't working at Twitter, why they're not building the tech. You're more interested in, like, okay, they're not doing anything, how have we been protecting ourselves?"

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: So, for me. I really started to lean in on that, in particular. And throughout my doc program, I just spent a lot of time doing a lot of, like, public scholarship talks and things like that, really, like massaging and theorizing and talking through these things with folks in any space that would listen, and it really helped me figure out exactly how I wanted to do my study, because when Megan Thee Stallion was shot in 2020, it was the… the most palatable example, for people who ignored what happened to Leslie Jones, to understand that celebrity does not remove you from misogynoir online.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: So, I spent a lot of time, like, scraping, (this is before Elon bought it), but scraping a lot of tweets, of what people were saying, screenshot, doing talks, using hip-hop feminism in particular as one of my foundational theories to talk about this idea, that Gwendolyn Pugh talks about in her book, "Bringing Wreck," called, she talks about, like, bringing wreck, like, this idea of sass, right? Sass as a form of resistance, right? I talked about the lineage of that becoming "clapping back."

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: So, my entire research focuses on how the clapback is a part of these other harm reduction strategies that I uncovered during my interviews and my autoethnography of how Black women are protecting themselves and intervening in these spaces that do not have any of the tools or the people that do it for them. So, in my, dissertation, and I can email it to you, it is embargoed, but I… you can read it, and I can send you my master's thesis publication, I had all of these, like thematic codes. So, like, higher order codes from the particular interviews, and I only did 16, because that's when I kind of reached saturation, and each particular higher order code focus on different elements that came up, and I'm gonna pull up the dissertation so I can, like, say them verbatim. But for that particular, part of, like, my findings and my dissertation, I wanted to make sure that when I was doing, like, my coding and my thematic analysis, that I was also paying close attention, because I think I did, like, inductive and deductive coding, so I had, like, a list of codes, but I also had, like, codes that I was… like, that would come up. But what was important to me was that I wanted to make sure that the themes that came out of the data could be clearly explained using direct quotes from my participants.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: Because one of the things that I noticed a lot when people were writing about Black women's experiences online, because around this time, this is when Moya's book came out, Safiya's book came out, "Hood Feminism" had came out, "America, Goddam", "Distributed Blackness," and it's like, all of their books were coming out around this time, right? So, I got all this stuff, I'm like, great, now I can start citing these people. But also in community with them. And no one was talking about digital misogynoir. Like, digital misogynoir was not a terminology that was being used. Moya Bailey made it very clear that misogynoir shows up in U.S. digital and visual culture, but because of the fact that I was always interested in, like, the online experience, I was like, I need to make sure that when I am doing this coding, and I'm writing these themes out, that these themes can actually encompass not only, like, my work, but the work of those before me, and also can be something that can be used as maybe, like, policy or action items that paint, like, the whole picture, and not just, like, the picture of, oh, you know, Black women have been so harmed online.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: It's more so, like, yes. They've been harmed online. Also, and they're also creating communities online, right? They're also still using these platforms, right? That is something that I had to make very clear that, like they are still using these platforms, so…

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: My, themes were, the higher order code of that theme was digital self-defense and harm reduction tactics, so… How, like, digital misogynoir, cyber feminism, and technological empowerment, cultural production and representation, and then reclaiming digital spaces, and I used a lot of the work from, Seyi Akiwowo. She has a book, and she used to… she founded Glitch UK. I used a lot of Moya's work, Kishonna Gray's work, a lot of even Feminista Jones' book, which talks about this, like, reclaiming, to kind of, like, guide, right, how I was analyzing it.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: And then the second higher order coder theme was critical consciousness and empowerment, which I was excited the most about because it focused on community, solidarity, and sisterhood, but it also talked about the matrix of domination and oppression, and controlling images and stereotypes, and how these things also were showing up online through these conversations that I was having with these hundreds of Black women and non-binary folks across the diaspora, might I add you. I wasn't just talking to people here in the U.S. I was talking wherever there was a homegirl located, I did a wide cast net.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: And then the last theme was the outcomes of the algorithm, and I talked about social media, but the shift of protection, specifically looking at what happened when Elon Musk purchased it, and what shifts Black women saw. Violence and negative moments, how those particular things impact the experience, whether they are experiencing it, or witnessing it. Because a lot of times, what I noticed in the earlier research, a lot of folks weren't talking about, like, what it feels like to witness it. Right? Like, what does it feel like to watch Black women be attacked online? Talked about the physiological impacts, which I hadn't seen a lot on. I know in Treva B. Lindsay's book, "America, Goddam," she talks about that a lot, but what actually happens when a Black woman experiences or sees misogynoir online, right? And I was able to get raw data of the actual physical symptoms that Black women were experiencing.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: And then the lack of recourse was the last part. We're focusing on, at that time, that there is literally no consequence, there is no pathway, there is no policy, there is no work being done to actually fix this in real time. And I think that, like… That part of my research informed a lot of when I think about harm reduction. So, like, the things that they would do that people weren't even naming, right? Whether it's, like, making your profile photo a housewife, or meme, so no one knows what you look like. So if they drag you, they can't go to your photos and be like, "this you?" Like, these very small things that people are, like, not thinking about, right? Or, like, people not posting what they're doing in real time, right? Which people talk about a lot now, but, like people not posting when they are going on vacations. Black women being very, very, like, intentional, right, with not posting those particular things. Using aliases, right? Also, like, being very, like, mindful of what they're sharing about themselves online as a form of harm reduction so they can enjoy being online. Even, like, not responding to certain type of, like, rage engagement or rage baiting depended on the size of that person's platform. Right? Like, responding to someone who has a large platform is dangerous, right? Not, like… Creating group chats, going offline to tell people, can you all go report this person? They're harming someone. Right? These are all things that are tactics that Black women and nonbinary femmes are doing in real time that are not baked into the actual moderation and the tooling that we see on social media platforms.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Yeah, wow. That's such a beautiful response, and I feel like it connects so well, too, with, like, how you were describing Blackness, in the sense that it's, like, there is this rage and deep sadness existing on these platforms where people feel comfortable being incredibly anti-Black. And being incredibly misogynistic, and… I don't know the right way to conjugate this, but, like, misogynoiristic… Yeah.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: So, misogynoiristic, yeah.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Yeah. But then, at the same time, having the faith to… not just faith that something will come out of it, but to then, like use that to build the space, right? Like, so much of what gave Twitter its power was Black Twitter, and creating these sorts of, like, mechanisms for harm reduction through practice. And I think that that kind of ties directly into my next question of, like, what...

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Can you describe Blacksky for me, and how you found yourself in this space, yeah?

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: Yeah, so, I'll describe Blacksky. So, Blacksky is a… I consider it to be, like, a social media network that focuses on the foundational principles of Black liberation, Black feminism, organizing principles that really lean into self-governance, and also a very intentional community-led, community model that not only creates, like, this social media network where you can engage with folks and build community, but also creates the infrastructure and the tooling for you to be able to do those things.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: And in particular, Blacksky, which… what makes it very, very unique, is that because it is on a open social network, right, there is a lot more freedom to decide and work with in community on what digital liberation can look like, and be able to actually create the tooling to do the thing, right? There's a difference in theory and praxis, right? Right? So, like, a lot of things can live in theory, right? But for Blacksky in particular, Blacksky is actually putting those things into practice, and practice, right, by creating the tooling and giving people a clear understanding of what it means to actually have autonomy and sovereignty over your experiences online.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: And as far as, like, how I was introduced to Blacksky is that once I finished my doc program, I was already… I already had a full-time job. I was working the whole time, teaching and stuff like that. I had my own businesses. But I was already planning on deleting my Twitter anyway, because I just had too large of a following, my page was private. Like I, at that point, I had been on Twitter since, like, 2009. I was tired. It was, like, 2024 at the time. I was tired. I said, "you know what, y'all? There's nothing else I can do on this platform, so I'm out." And I'm also one of those people where I'll delete something and I don't even tell nobody. So it's just like, they're like, dang, KáLyn gone. But one of my good friends had posted something about Blacksky, but it wasn't, like, anything, like, very, like, detailed, but it was more so like, "oh, you know. I'm liking this Blacksky feed on Bluesky." And I was just like, girl, what's that? And she was like, oh, you can see it from your Bluesky account. So after I deleted my Twitter account, and I believe, like, November 2024, maybe, like, late October… it had to be November 2024, I was like, I think… I was like, oh yeah, I think I do have a Bluesky account, because I got an invite code. So I, like, logged back in, and the first thing I looked for was this, like, Blacksky feed to see what she was talking about. I saw the feed, I said, "oh, this is interesting."

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: And then I came across, I don't know how I came across it, but I came across, like, the Blacksky Moderation. And I literally was preparing to do a talk at VCU for their Humanities Research Center and Lab on, like my dream vision of creating a moderation tool, at this time, like, I was like, I am gonna have to use some type of, like LLM, or find a tech person, because I wasn't really sure, like, how I would be able to, like, trace it, and I wanted to be able to use… like, I wanted to be able to train whatever it was that I was using with, like, cultural nuanced language to be able to, like, identify misogynoir anti-Blackness. And I came across the page for, like, the moderation, and it said, like, it had, like, anti-Black harassment and misogynoir, and I said, "hold the fuck up. Who is this? Who doing this," right? Because you have to remember, I've been doing this research for so long, I literally was like at that point, like I said, the deep sadness and rage of faith, I literally had faith for the impossible. I couldn't explain exactly where it would live, I couldn't explain… like, I had a whole research proposal that I had wrote for this particular, like, type of moderation, this AI moderation, quote-unquote, because I was like, I'mma have to get research, I'mma have to get funding, like, I don't know…No one else has ever done this. That was another thing, too, like, even my mentors. People who are, like, legends in the game also were like, this is possible, we're not 100% sure where, but, like, keep dreaming about this.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: So I reached out to Rudy, and I was like, "Hi, my name is Dr. K, can I set up some time to meet with you?" So, him and I set up a meeting, I sent over, like, I think I sent over, like, some stuff that I had done, some work and some stuff, but I'm pretty sure Rudy might have, like, looked me up or something like that, because when we got on the call, I was like, "oh, I wanted to learn more about Blacksky and about moderation," and I was like, "you know, this is the type of research that I do, and I was like can I… can I volunteer?" Because in my head, I was like, oh, I just want to volunteer. I was like, "can I volunteer?" I was like, "I would love to see how y'all are moderating, because I've never been on the back end, like, looking at reports. I've only seen the front end of, like, what I would deem as misogynoir, or what, like would fall under the category of harassment from, like, my perspective." And he was like, yeah, sure. And he was like, "do you want to be… like, do you want to be public?" Because the other moderator at the time, he was like, you know, they're anonymous. And I was like, "abso-fucking-lutely."  I said, "for sure," I said "I don't care who knows that I'm moderating." I was… and I made clear, I was like, I've been getting doxed for a long time, like, this, for me, I don't care about none of this. Like, I am okay with, like, me being, like, known as, oh, this person's moderating.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: So I became the first, like, contracted moderator, moved to community safety and support steward after I did a lot of moderation, used a lot of, like, my research and learning to, like, inform over that first 9 months of volunteering of, like, expanding the labels from just those two labels to, like a whole suite of labels. Did a lot of user education around, like, what is misogynoir, what is anti-Blackness, having these conversations with folks, right? And continue to, like, do that on the side, along with, like, one of my own businesses and things like that, but, like, I was… it was very much so, like, a… a, like, passion… I don't want to say passion project, because it's a long, a long… this is, like, a sustainable long-term, company and infrastructure and community, but in that particular moment for me, I was like, I want to contribute in any way that I can, and provide impact, and I want to do it because it is… literally what I have been dreaming of trying to do. There's actually, like, as far as it comes to, like, jobs and stuff, like, I… When I first moved over there, I was like, I can do it for free, I don't care. Like, this is… for me, this is, like, something that I just need to be able to see how this works. See, like, if the… if the research that I've been doing, if the things that I've been reading, if the people that came before me, if what we're talking about is actually possible through what is being done at Blacksky.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: And that is kind of how I got introduced to, Blacksky, and was a moderator, community safety and support steward. Eventually, I was being tapped a lot by Rudy to do a lot of, like, the speaking and things like that, like, obviously, like, coming to MED Lab [Media Economies Design Lab], but just in general, doing, like, a lot of different speaking stuff, and it was perfect for me because I was already doing a lot of, like public scholarship and education around digital misogynoir, because people won't really talk about it still. It was really getting underneath my skin. So I was already, like, you know, being an evangelist with Moya Bailey's book across anywhere I could, so it was very, very, like, exciting to be able to talk about a tool at that time, that's now this independent, huge platform, right, that is actually doing what you motherfuckers said was impossible. But it wasn't impossible, you just didn't find it valuable. And done with no large backing of funding. Right? So that's how I got introduced into Blacksky.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: That's beautiful. I also really love how you talked about this emphasis on praxis, right? It's like, you took these ideas that you'd been talking about for so long in academia, and then you found this place where it's actually being done in a… a direct way that's, like, immediately impacting people's lives in a way where it's not just… not to say "not just," but, like... Being in academia right now, sometimes it can feel really frustrating to, like, have these really foundational ideas, and then… You know, it feels like… How can we make this… bring this out into the world in a very actionable way. So that's really beautiful.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: And I really appreciated how you talked about Blacksky having, like, this particular praxis that is oriented towards liberation, and so I'm curious about what that looks like on a few different fronts. So, first, like, what is the structure of Blacksky? Like, how is it governed? You know, I've seen things around, like, the People's Assembly. So on that front, but also in terms of, like, internally, what that kind of governance looks like.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: Yeah, so, the People's Assembly is definitely a democratic tooling that we use to have conversations with our community members. Because it is a open source platform, community members can also contribute code and fixes and even features, right? To be embedded into Blacksky. Like, we've had one community member, he created, like, the hiding… like, a hiding feature where you could hide a post by just pressing… clicking a little eye. We've had other folks who have just contributed, whether it was, like, information: we have another community member who created, like, a walkthrough video for when we were doing migrations to, like, explain how to do these things. And I think that because it is open source, but also because, Rudy was very intentional early on when he made the feed back in 2023, and, like, you know, rolled out this labeler, that, like, you know, like, this is actually, like essentially, like, a community project, like, we all doing this together, and, like, that really set the tone for Blacksky as it stands today.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: And it still informs how we do stuff as a team internally. So, we currently all became full-time over the summer, on Juneteenth to be exact, which I thought was very cute. And, you know, and now we have, like, more staff members, we have a full staff, and one of the things that, is really, really, like, a through line is, like how will… how will this impact the community members? And not just the community members, right, that are just using the app, but also the developers who are using our code, right? So, our code "rsky," even, like, our... our relays, our servers, like, other people on the protocol are using the tech that we've built, the tech that has been created, for their own projects and communities and things like that, right? So when we're thinking about what we're going to be implementing, when we're thinking about what type of features, when we're thinking about, like the types of decisions that we make that may, like, really directly impact or shift the experience for not only just the users and the community members, but also those, those folks that are developers in the ecosystem, right, doing their own projects, we have to always go back to thinking about that.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: And also having that transparency, right, with our community members with the ecosystem, with the protocol, about sometimes some of the things that we're thinking through, even if that transparency can lead to contentious conversations.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: Like, we, earlier this year, there was a very intense conversation around, like, if we were to release Blacksky-only posts. Like, there is a world where we may have to do, like, AI moderation, right? And we needed to talk to everybody about that, and, like, it was a very, very heavily contentious, engaged conversation amongst folks, and we had to, like, obviously look at what they were saying, have a lot of internal conversations, really think about, like, what this… what… what this could look like if we had these different types of options. We presented different options, they were able to vote on it in the People's Assembly, right? But we also made it clear that, like… And this is another thing that I think is very, true to, like the user-facing side and the developer-facing side versus internally is that very clear that, like, shit can change, right? So, like, we will always come back to the drawing board to have discussions about what's working, what's not working, what can be fixed better, like, what does it look like if we do this? And I think that that is something that has always been, like, embedded in, like, the fabric of Blacksky, dealing with the community, and we are, you know, working continuously as we are building this team, and, you know, getting to learn each other's working styles, and, you know, understanding that, like, the stakes were always high, right? But now we have even larger, you know, goals on app adoption, and, like, creating more tools, and, like, letting people know about the type of infrastructure that we've built for those who are not on the protocol, right? So this leaves, like, that part in, like, building, like, a coalition, and that starts with how we started engaging with the community, taking those particular learnings into how we are trying to grow and shape our own internal culture, so that way, as we're trying to build this coalition of other value-aligned folks in all different types of spaces, we are all on the same page of... "the foundation is community."

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: That's, like, the bottom line. Obviously, like, people gotta eat, people got bills, that's very clear, but there are still checks and balances, there are still things that we have to fully, deeply discuss, right? And those decisions that we're making, right, as a team, come from the way that Rudy fostered early on with the Blacksky Feed the needs of community, those organizing principles that most of us on the team share.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Yeah, I really love, love that, like, the way that you are tying the sort of technological, like philosophy around how you engage with technology to that wider mission and praxis. Earlier, you mentioned "Distributed Blackness," and so I'm curious about how you would define distribution, or, like, "distributed" in this sense, when you're thinking about, like your work and Blacksky more broadly.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: Hmm, let me think… I have to make sure that I speak correctly, just in case André hears this and fusses at me. Because André knows how I feel about that book. It's too hard! I'm sorry, like, I've never in my life read a book, and was, like, talking to the person, like, what? What? What is… I need… I need you to explain it to me like a fifth grader. But… what I will say is that I think that it is… it's so funny, I literally have, like, the book right here with my little notes, like, on my bookshelf beside me. What I will say is that when I think about, like, how Blacksky is kind of, like distributing Blackness, I think a lot about, like, ancestral technology, right? And this idea, and like André talked about, a lot of people in the space Black folks talk about, right? This… this idea of, like, how… how we've distributed Blackness How we have… alchemized, right? Created, right? Subverted, right? Things… And all of these different spaces are actually, like, ingrained in us as a people, right? And for me, I truly believe that, the internet, in particular, exposes all of those… the ways in which all of these, like, ancestral learnings and this ancestral technology did a number on some folks, whether it was positive or negative, right? Thinking about respectability politics, right? A lot of the things that we've always seen in the Black community in these digital spaces, and specifically in Blacksky, are being addressed and talked about, right? But also, there is a… a very particular way that Black people do discourse online, That is very much so deeply, like critical to how we see tech today. So I always, like, a lot of people always say, is Black Twitter and Blacksky the same? And I'm like, no, as someone who actually, like, studied Black Twitter, is, like, a mentee of those folks, like, it is not the same, but there is a pathway, right?

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: So when we think about, like Anna Everett's book, "The Digital Diaspora," when she's talking about, like, the digital divide back in the 90s, and, like, the Million Woman March, and how they had a forum online, and the harassment there, right? And we're, like, traveling through, like, when we think about, like, the blogging era, right? When we think about, you know all these other different forums, you know, or these websites, like Black Planet, or Black Gay Chat, like, all these things, or Crush Spot, MySpace, and we get into, like, Twitter, and then we have Black Twitter, right? All of these instances of Blacknesses… Blackness in this digital space kind of shaped how we have been continuously, like, distributing this ancestral technology throughout these different instances, and where we're at now with Blacksky, I always say that, like, Black Twitter really was a firm reminder that we actually, control how discourse moves. We control how communities are built. Especially in digital spaces, and that also requires us to have very, very, very, very, very uncomfortable conversations that may not have been had, right? At the family cookout, right? It may not have been had with folks in the church, right? But because we're on the internet, and a lot of people have access to it, all types of Black people, right? This particular, like way of thinking, being, knowing, communicating is ongoing, constantly evolving, constantly being revisited, right? Constantly, like being interrogated in a way that I would say, for Blacksky in particular, where there are tools to also keep those conversations as safe as possible, right?

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: So on Black Twitter, like I talked about, like, on Twitter in general, like, we created our own harm reduction strategies, right? But that trauma and experience that specifically those Black women, even myself, experienced on Twitter have deeply shaped how we engage with social media today, 10 years, 10, 11 years later, and it requires a level of grace, a level of, sensitivity and a level of patience when building something like Blacksky, especially, like, from where I sit as head of community and research, is that having to create a long-standing trust with people who have historically experienced the worst of the worst in these digital spaces, in all different formats, from all different kinds of people, and trying to truly basically help them unlearn, right, that, like, there is a way for you to have power and sovereignty. There is a way for us to have these hard conversations that don't lead to it just being a cycle of the same conversation, because there's no way to actually mitigate that harm, right? That it's okay for people to be "both, and," even if it's uncomfortable.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: It makes me think about Joan Morgan's, like, "fucking with the grays" with hip-hop feminism that I talked about earlier. I feel like, you know, really thinking about, like, the like, cyber culture, and how it's constantly evolving, and, like, revisiting things, and the conversations, and, like, the new information that we are learning about how to identify, how to call out, how to categorize, right, how to protect, is very, very cyclical in nature. And as the internet continues to grow, we have to look back at, like, the actual historical legacies of race in the internet to understand, like, what the… how the conversations sometimes are the same, sometimes are different, but just how the tech really does change how we distribute, how we experience Blackness, what Blackness looks like in these different cybercultures.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: There's so much here that I feel like I'm gonna end up pulling into my research more largely, so I really appreciate that. Both within Blacksky, but also just writ large, like, as people. Why do we need community?

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: Yeah, so I… My own… my personal philosophy is that I'm not self-made, every accomplishment, every accolade, everything that I've been able to do has been done in community. I even, like, I think I wrote, like, a long, like, write-up on this, so where, like, like, community, for me, is very much so… Understanding that community doesn't always feel good. Community doesn't always… community isn't, like, a yes… like, a yes-man, right, thing. Like, community is a bit of push and pull. It is very much so, being able to challenge and also affirm.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: It's also very rooted in understanding that, like, if I'm experiencing something, if I'm experiencing trauma, right, that… that does impact my community as well, right? So when our community are experiencing these things, even if they may not be directly connected to our own lived experiences, as a community, it does impact us. Like, I was talking about earlier, about, like subconsciously, whether you don't believe it or not, like, these things are impacting you.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: And in order to be in community with folks, you have to really fully understand that, like community doesn't always mean that these people are your people, one, right? Community can look like that you are moving through different communities based on where you're at in your life, right? What works for you. It can mean that you don't gotta be friends with every Black person you come into contact with. That's not what community means, right? Like, you definitely should not be forcing yourself to be in community with people who seek to harm you. Like, that is a non-negotiable.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: But when it comes to community, if I personally have a resource that I think is helpful, and I do have a way to get it to them, I'mma give it to them, right? If I am okay with the fact that I actually do not give two fucks about Talib Kweli, right? And how he treats Black women, and you can put this on record, I don't care, like, he know I'm out for him. I am very aware of the fact that he could very much so experience police brutality as a Black man, right? That, to me, is community-minded. Now, does that mean then I'm gonna take that misogynoir label off his page? Absolutely the fuck not, right? Because you're harming Black women, but I'm not going to ever agree with community, you know, being, like, just exerting energy to be malicious to someone else. Like, other people can handle your light work, right? Like, I do believe in revenge and all types of things, but, like, from a community mindset, I personally am not going out of my way to make you know that, like I don't consider you to be with community, you'll feel that, right?

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: And I also think that community is realizing that you're gonna sometimes feel alone, right? You're gonna also have to hold yourself accountable for how you treat your community members. Even if you felt that you were right at that time, it's gonna require you to sometimes shut the fuck up, right? Because your voice is not the voice that should be taking up the space at that moment. It's gonna require a bit of humility, and I don't mean, like, being humble and, like, downplaying yourself, but humility in the fact that, like, your lived experience is important, but your lived experience is not the only experience when you are in community. And that everyone is beholden to their community in some way, especially their chosen community, right? The people that you choose to be in community with, and you're accountable to them, and they're accountable to you. And that is not easy work.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: And I think as it pertains to Blacksky, I think that because this idea of community can be subjective, I, from where I… from where I sit, I can't speak for Blacksky as a company, or what Rudy thinks, or maybe other, employees think, but I think that what Blacksky is doing is giving people options, autonomy, sovereignty, to decide what they want their communities to look like. That is not our decision, right? Like, how you want to, how you want to, like, self-govern. Self is the key word, right? Like, how you, like, when we're doing the People's Assembly, like, we are encouraging you to input your perspective from where your vantage point is, and to see the consensus amongst your community members, right? I'm not trying to shape, right? What you think is the best way to be in community.

speaker: Dr. KáLyn Coghill
words: What I think that Blacksky is definitely doing is giving people the tools and access, the tooling, to be able to experience digital liberation in a way that will and want… will encourage them to want to engage in community building in a way that has been lost for a long time. On a lot of different platforms, just due to the nature of the amount of violence and harm that exists in those spaces at the same time, to where you don't really have time sometimes to actually have these discussions, to discuss them, to vote on them, to do polls, to, like, really think about, like, mutual aid. Like, these are things that, like, are constantly being communicated and talked about amongst the community member, along with all types of foolish stuff, too, right? Both can exist, right? And I think that's how Blacksky is, really, like showing folks what it means to be in community, and also that, like, community is a… it is a process of effort, is a process of hard conversations, and it's a process of accountability both ways.
